claim: AKAP79 increases the rate of calcineurin dephosphorylation of type II PKA regulatory subunits by an order of magnitude.
source: In this study, we discovered that AKAP79 increases the rate of calcineurin dephosphorylation of type II PKA regulatory subunits by an order of magnitude.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D demonstrating 12.4-fold and 16.3-fold increases in dephosphorylation rates for RIIα and RIIβ respectively.

claim: AKAP79-enhanced calcineurin activity enables suppression of PKA without altering cAMP levels by increasing PKA catalytic subunit capture rate.
source: Fluorescent PKA activity reporter assays, supported by kinetic modeling, show how AKAP79-enhanced calcineurin activity enables suppression of PKA without altering cAMP levels by increasing PKA catalytic subunit capture rate.
evidence: Supported by AKAR4 fluorescence assays (Figure 3) and kinetic modeling (Figure 4) showing reduced PKA activity in the presence of AKAP79 and CN.

claim: The mechanism of AKAP79-mediated PKA suppression by calcineurin contributes toward long-term depression (LTD).
source: Experiments with hippocampal neurons indicate that this mechanism contributes toward LTD.
evidence: Supported by chemical LTD experiments in hippocampal neurons (Figure 6) showing that mutations preventing RII phosphorylation state regulation reduce LTD.

claim: cAMP and Ca2+ are ancient second messengers fundamental to the regulation of many dynamic cellular processes including synaptic plasticity.
source: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and Ca2+ are ancient second messengers that are fundamental to the regulation of many dynamic cellular processes including synaptic plasticity (Huang et al., 1994), heart contraction (Bers et al., 2019), and glycogen metabolism (Roach et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on cAMP and Ca2+ signaling.

claim: cAMP can enhance cytosolic Ca2+ entry by triggering phosphorylation of key ion channels by PKA.
source: For example, cAMP can enhance cytosolic Ca2+ entry by triggering phosphorylation of key ion channels (Qian et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2003) by its major intracellular receptor cAMP-dependent protein kinase, also known as Protein Kinase A (PKA).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on cAMP-mediated ion channel regulation.

claim: Ca2+ can regulate cAMP levels by altering activities of both phosphodiesterases and adenylyl cyclases.
source: Similarly, Ca2+ can regulate cAMP levels by altering activities of both phosphodiesterases (Baillie et al., 2019) and adenylyl cyclases (Qi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on Ca2+-mediated regulation of cAMP metabolism.

claim: A common signaling motif is the opposition of PKA and the Ca2+-sensitive phosphatase calcineurin.
source: At the receptor level, a common signaling motif is the opposition of PKA and the highly abundant Ca2+-sensitive phosphatase calcineurin (CN), with CN triggering cellular changes by removing phosphate from substrates primed by PKA.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of PKA-calcineurin signaling dynamics.

claim: Calcineurin triggers cellular changes by removing phosphate from substrates primed by PKA in the regulation of postsynaptic substrates including AMPA-type glutamate receptors in LTD induction.
source: Notable examples of this motif are the regulation of postsynaptic substrates including AMPA-type glutamate receptors in the induction of long-term depression (LTD) of synaptic strength (Bear, 2003), and control of NFAT nuclear localization in immune responses (Hogan, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on LTD and NFAT regulation.

claim: According to current consensus, calcineurin dephosphorylates substrates without any requirement for directly altering PKA activity.
source: According to current consensus, in these cases CN dephosphorylates substrates without any requirement for directly altering PKA activity (Dittmer et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2011; Tunquist et al., 2008; Weisenhaus et al., 2010; Zhang and Shapiro, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies representing the current consensus view.

claim: The current model implies that energetically costly futile cycles of phosphate addition and removal by PKA and CN must persist to maintain dephosphorylated substrate.
source: This implies that energetically costly futile cycles of phosphate addition and removal by PKA and CN must persist to maintain dephosphorylated substrate.
evidence: Logical inference from the current consensus model of PKA-CN signaling.

claim: It would be more logical for PKA activity to be switched off when CN is activated during substrate dephosphorylation.
source: It would be more logical for PKA activity to be switched off when CN is activated during substrate dephosphorylation.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about a more efficient signaling mechanism.

claim: PKA is comprised of regulatory subunit dimers that bind and sequester PKA catalytic (C) subunits in an inhibited state.
source: PKA is comprised of regulatory subunit dimers that bind and sequester PKA catalytic (C) subunits in an inhibited state (Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on PKA structure.

claim: PKA regulatory subunits are classified into type I subunits (RIα and RIβ) that are predominantly cytosolic, and type II subunits (RIIα and RIIβ) that co-sediment with membranes.
source: PKA regulatory subunits are classified into type I subunits (RIα and RIβ) that are predominantly cytosolic, and type II subunits (RIIα and RIIβ) that co-sediment with membranes (Gold, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published review on PKA localization.

claim: The regulatory subunit inhibitor sequence (IS) is phosphorylated upon association with C subunits for RII but not RI subunits.
source: The regulatory subunit inhibitor sequence (IS) is phosphorylated upon association with C subunits for RII but not RI subunits, which bear alanine in place of serine in the phospho-acceptor site (S98 in RIIα).
evidence: Established knowledge about PKA regulatory subunit phosphorylation.

claim: PKA regulatory subunits, particularly RII subunits, greatly outnumber PKA C subunits throughout the body.
source: Quantitative immunoblotting and mass spectrometry (MS) have recently shown that PKA regulatory subunits – and particularly RII subunits – greatly outnumber PKA C subunits (Aye et al., 2010; Walker-Gray et al., 2017) throughout the body.
evidence: Supported by citations to published quantitative studies on PKA subunit stoichiometry.

claim: The kon rate for C subunit association is ~50 times faster for dephosphorylated RII than pRII.
source: Remarkably, the kon rate for C subunit association is ~50 times faster for dephosphorylated RII than pRII (Zhang et al., 2015; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to published kinetic study and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Rapid dephosphorylation of RII subunits by CN could directly suppress PKA activity by increasing the rate of C subunit capture.
source: In theory, rapid dephosphorylation of RII subunits by CN could directly suppress PKA activity by increasing the rate of C subunit capture thereby reducing the proportion of C subunits that are dissociated (Buxbaum and Dudai, 1989; Isensee et al., 2018; Ogreid and Døskeland, 1981; Stemmer and Klee, 1994; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Theoretical mechanism supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Isolated pRII is a low-affinity substrate for CN with a half-maximal substrate concentration (Km) above 20 µM.
source: While recent observations concerning PKA subunit stoichiometry and pRII/RII binding kinetics support this notion, isolated pRII is a low-affinity substrate for CN with a half-maximal substrate concentration (Km) above 20 µM (Blumenthal et al., 1986; Perrino et al., 1992; Stemmer and Klee, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to published kinetic studies on CN-pRII interactions.

claim: pRII dephosphorylation by CN would not be expected to occur to a meaningful degree at physiological concentrations in the absence of an additional factor.
source: Therefore, pRII dephosphorylation by CN would not be expected to occur to a meaningful degree at physiological concentrations in the absence of an additional factor.
evidence: Inference based on the low affinity of CN for isolated pRII.

claim: AKAP79 can simultaneously anchor both CN and PKA.
source: AKAP79 can simultaneously anchor both CN and PKA (Coghlan et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on AKAP79 binding partners.

claim: AKAP79 contains an amphipathic anchoring helix for binding RII subunits.
source: It contains an amphipathic anchoring helix (Gold et al., 2006; Kinderman et al., 2006) for binding RII subunits, and a short linear 'PIAIIIT' CN anchoring motif (Dell'Acqua et al., 2002; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies on AKAP79.

claim: The CN and RII anchoring sites in AKAP79 are separated by only ~50 amino acids in the primary sequence within the C-terminus.
source: The two anchoring sites are separated by only ~50 amino acids in the primary sequence within the C-terminus of AKAP79 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Structural information illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: AKAP79 is localized in dendritic spines where it is required for anchoring RII subunits.
source: AKAP79 is localized in dendritic spines where it is required for anchoring RII subunits (Tunquist et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on AKAP79 localization and function.

claim: AKAP79 is necessary for both induction of long-term depression (LTD) of CA3-CA1 hippocampal synapses.
source: The anchoring protein is necessary for both induction of long-term depression (LTD) of CA3-CA1 hippocampal synapses (Lu et al., 2008; Tunquist et al., 2008; Weisenhaus et al., 2010), and for CN-mediated dephosphorylation of NFAT (Kar et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2014) – both processes that are driven by CN dephosphorylation of sites primed by PKA.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on AKAP79 function in LTD and NFAT regulation.

claim: AKAP79 acts as a weak inhibitor for CN dephosphorylation of 20-mer peptides corresponding to the phosphorylated RII IS.
source: Despite these characteristics, the possibility that AKAP79 could support pRII dephosphorylation by CN has been disregarded perhaps because paradoxically AKAP79 acts as a weak inhibitor for CN dephosphorylation of 20-mer peptides corresponding to the phosphorylated RII IS (Coghlan et al., 1995; Kashishian et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on AKAP79 effects on CN activity toward peptides.

claim: Inclusion of full-length AKAP79 increased phosphate release from pRIIα by 12.4-fold compared to pRIIα without AKAP79.
source: Inclusion of full-length AKAP79 in the reaction mix increased phosphate release by 12.4-fold (P = 7.4 × 10–6) to 4.52% ± 0.26 % pRIIα subunits (light blue, Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with statistical significance.

claim: Removing the PIAIIIT anchoring sequence in AKAP79 (ΔCN) returned dephosphorylation to baseline level.
source: Removing the PIAIIIT anchoring sequence in AKAP79 (ΔCN) returned dephosphorylation to a baseline level of 0.26% ± 0.06 % (gray, Figure 1C), consistent with a mechanism in which anchoring of CN adjacent to pRII subunits enhances the rate of dephosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating the requirement for the CN anchoring motif.

claim: Addition of AKAP79 increased phosphate release from pRIIβ by 16.3-fold.
source: Similar results were obtained for pRIIβ, with addition of AKAP79 increasing phosphate release 16.3-fold (p = 3.0 × 10–6) from 0.34% ± 0.13 % (black, Figure 1D) to 5.49% ± 0.17 % (dark blue, Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance.

claim: pRIIα-AKAP79c97 was dephosphorylated with a Km of 1.36 ± 0.16 µM and kcat of 0.45 ± 0.02 s–1.
source: pRIIα-AKAP79c97 (light blue, Figure 1E) was dephosphorylated with a half-maximal concentration (Km) of 1.36 ± 0.16 µM and turnover number (kcat) of 0.45 ± 0.02 s–1, and pRIIβ-AKAP79c97 with Km = 0.74 ± 0.12 µM and kcat = 0.24 ± 0.01 s–1.
evidence: Supported by kinetic measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: pRIIβ-AKAP79c97 was dephosphorylated with Km = 0.74 ± 0.12 µM and kcat = 0.24 ± 0.01 s–1.
source: pRIIα-AKAP79c97 (light blue, Figure 1E) was dephosphorylated with a half-maximal concentration (Km) of 1.36 ± 0.16 µM and turnover number (kcat) of 0.45 ± 0.02 s–1, and pRIIβ-AKAP79c97 with Km = 0.74 ± 0.12 µM and kcat = 0.24 ± 0.01 s–1.
evidence: Supported by kinetic measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In the absence of AKAP79, pRIIα and pRIIβ subunits served as low affinity substrates for CN with Km greater than 20 µM.
source: As expected, in the absence of the anchoring protein, pRIIα and pRIIβ subunits served as low affinity substrates for CN (black lines, Figure 1E & F). For both isolated pRII isoforms, the relationship between phosphatase activity and pRII concentration was linear up to 20 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) – the highest concentration tested – indicative of a Km of greater than 20 µM.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E, 1F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: WT AKAP79c97 enhanced CN activity toward pNPP by ~65%.
source: WT AKAP79c97 enhanced CN activity toward pNPP by ~65%, and reduced its activity towards pRII phosphopeptide by ~50%, consistent with previous reports that AKAP79 acts as a weak inhibitor of CN activity toward this phosphopeptide (Coghlan et al., 1995; Kashishian et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: WT AKAP79c97 reduced CN activity towards pRII phosphopeptide by ~50%.
source: WT AKAP79c97 enhanced CN activity toward pNPP by ~65%, and reduced its activity towards pRII phosphopeptide by ~50%, consistent with previous reports that AKAP79 acts as a weak inhibitor of CN activity toward this phosphopeptide (Coghlan et al., 1995; Kashishian et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: AKAP79 enhances CN dephosphorylation of full-length RII subunits by increasing effective substrate concentration rather than by altering the inherent catalytic activity of the phosphatase.
source: Overall, our data are consistent with a mechanism in which AKAP79 enhances CN dephosphorylation of full-length RII subunits by increasing effective substrate concentration rather than by altering the inherent catalytic activity of the phosphatase.
evidence: Inference based on the combined experimental data from Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: RIIα was the most predominant PKA subunit in the CA1 neuropil, accounting for 0.32% ± 0.029 % total protein content.
source: We found that RIIα was by far the most predominant PKA subunit in the CA1 neuropil, accounting for 0.32% ± 0.029 % total protein content compared to 0.032% ± 0.003 % for C subunits, 0.041% ± 0.014 % for RI, and 0.06% ± 0.006 % for RIIβ.
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: C subunits account for 0.032% ± 0.003 % of total protein content in CA1 neuropil.
source: We found that RIIα was by far the most predominant PKA subunit in the CA1 neuropil, accounting for 0.32% ± 0.029 % total protein content compared to 0.032% ± 0.003 % for C subunits, 0.041% ± 0.014 % for RI, and 0.06% ± 0.006 % for RIIβ.
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: There is a 9.4-fold higher molar abundance of RIIα subunits relative to C subunits in CA1 neuropil.
source: These numbers equate to a 9.4-fold higher molar abundance of RIIα subunits (light blue, Figure 2D) relative to C subunits with RI and RIIβ present at similar levels to C subunits.
evidence: Calculated from quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The estimated RII subunit concentrations are 5.9 µM (RIIα) and 1.03 µM (RIIβ) in CA1 neuropil.
source: Assuming that protein accounts for 8% of total rat brain weight (Clouet and Gaitonde, 1956), we estimated RII subunit concentrations of 5.9 µM (RIIα) and 1.03 µM (RIIβ).
evidence: Calculated from quantitative immunoblotting data with assumption about protein content cited from literature.

claim: The estimated RII subunit concentrations fall within the range where CN efficiently dephosphorylates pRII only in the presence of AKAP79.
source: These values fall within the range where CN efficiently dephosphorylates pRII only in the presence of AKAP79 (Figure 1E & F).
evidence: Inference connecting the measured physiological concentrations to the kinetic data in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: CN cannot efficiently dephosphorylate the AKAR4 reporter.
source: Importantly, supplementing these reactions with 1.5 μM activated CN had no detectable effect on AKAR4 phosphorylation rates, indicating that the phosphatase cannot efficiently dephosphorylate the reporter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C & D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: PP1 reduced the AKAR4 phosphorylation rate by ~7-fold.
source: In comparison, supplementation with 1.5 μM protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) reduced the phosphorylation rate by ~7-fold (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A & B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: CN exhibits very limited activity towards pre-phosphorylated AKAR4.
source: Phosphatase assays using pre-phosphorylated AKAR4 confirmed that CN exhibits very limited activity towards the reporter (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C & D), such that the reporter is well suited for experiments focusing on direct suppression of PKA activity by CN.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and 2D.

claim: At 1 µM cAMP activation, addition of both CN and AKAP79c97 reduced the initial rate of AKAR4 phosphorylation by 2.8-fold.
source: For example, with 1 µM cAMP activation, addition of both CN and the AKAP reduced the initial rate of AKAR4 phosphorylation by 2.8-fold from 18.9 ± 0.6 to 6.7% ± 0.8% per minute (p = 0.0007, black and red bars, Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D with statistical significance.

claim: Removing either the CN or PKA anchoring sites from AKAP79 abolished its ability to suppress PKA activity.
source: Similar AKAR4 responses were obtained when either the AKAP was omitted altogether (blue, Figure 3E & F), or if either the CN (purple) or PKA (orange) anchoring sites in the AKAP were removed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3F comparing WT and mutant AKAP79c97.

claim: AKAP79 and CN together reduced the proportion of free C subunits from 47.8 ± 1.5 to 20.2% ± 0.8% at 1 µM cAMP.
source: Together, AKAP79 and CN reduced the proportion of free C subunits at equilibrium across the cAMP concentration range including from 47.8 ± 1.5 to 20.2% ± 0.8% at 1 µM cAMP, and from 65.7 ± 1.1 to 33.2% ± 3.3% at 2 μM cAMP (Figure 4A & C).
evidence: Calculated from AKAR4 data cross-referenced to calibration curves, shown in Figure 4A and 4C.

claim: AKAP79 and CN together reduced the proportion of free C subunits from 65.7 ± 1.1 to 33.2% ± 3.3% at 2 μM cAMP.
source: Together, AKAP79 and CN reduced the proportion of free C subunits at equilibrium across the cAMP concentration range including from 47.8 ± 1.5 to 20.2% ± 0.8% at 1 µM cAMP, and from 65.7 ± 1.1 to 33.2% ± 3.3% at 2 μM cAMP (Figure 4A & C).
evidence: Calculated from AKAR4 data cross-referenced to calibration curves, shown in Figure 4A and 4C.

claim: The kinetic model indicates that AKAP79 and CN together shift C subunit capture to the faster dephosphorylated RII sub-system.
source: The model indicates that AKAP79 and CN together shift C subunit capture to the faster right-hand square sub-system (Figure 4D), driving down the fraction of free C subunits and thereby reducing PKA activity.
evidence: Inference from kinetic modeling results shown in Figure 4D-G.

claim: Substituting in RIIα S98A generated slow rates of AKAR4 phosphorylation regardless of CN presence.
source: Substituting in RIIα S98A generated slow rates of AKAR4 phosphorylation in both cases (6.30% ± 0.44 % per min with CN, and 6.67% ± 0.56 % without, Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The peak rate of AKAR4 phosphorylation was high regardless of CN presence for the RIIα S98E variant.
source: Conversely, the peak rate of AKAR4 phosphorylation was high regardless of the presence of CN for the S98E RIIα variant (31.30% ± 3.60 % per min without CN; 25.65% ± 3.44 % with CN, Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Substituting in either S98A or S98E RIIα in neurons would be expected to reduce LTD induction if direct suppression of PKA by CN is required.
source: Together, this data indicates that substituting in either mutant of RIIα in neurons would be expected to reduce LTD induction in neurons if direct suppression of PKA by CN is required in LTD induction (Figure 5E).
evidence: Inference from AKAR4 data with mutant RIIα predicting neuronal outcomes.

claim: Spine density was reduced by 33.5% in neurons expressing the RIIα S97A variant compared to WT RIIα.
source: Consistent with a role for PKA in spinogenesis, spine density was reduced by 33.5 % (p = 0.002) in neurons expressing the S97A variant to 1.17 ± 0.11 spines per 10 μm compared to 1.76 ± 0.12 for WT RIIα.
evidence: Supported by spine imaging data shown in Figure 6C and 6D with statistical significance.

claim: Bath application of 20 μM NMDA for 3 min triggered a 20.4% ± 1.6% reduction in spines after one hour in neurons expressing WT RIIα.
source: Bath application of 20 μM NMDA for 3 min triggered a steady reduction in spine density (Figure 6E, top row) in neurons expressing WT RIIα as expected (Zhou et al., 2004), reaching a 20.4% ± 1.6%% reduction in spines after one hour (blue, Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: Spine loss was attenuated in neurons expressing either the S97A or S97E RIIα variants.
source: In comparison, spine loss was attenuated in neurons expressing either the S97A (Figure 6E, middle row) or S97E (bottom row) RIIα variants.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: Spine numbers were reduced by only 9.07% ± 0.96 % in neurons expressing RIIα S97A.
source: Spine numbers were reduced by only 9.07% ± 0.96 % in neurons expressing RIIα S97A (red line, Figure 6F), and by 9.90% ± 1.8 % for the S97E variant (green line).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Attenuation of spine loss in neurons expressing either S97A or S97E RIIα is consistent with an important role for direct PKA activity suppression by CN during LTD induction.
source: Overall, attenuation of spine loss in neurons expressing either S97A (p = 0.00046) or S97E ( = 0.0014) RIIα compared to WT subunits is consistent with an important role for direct PKA activity suppression by CN during the induction of LTD.
evidence: Inference from neuronal LTD experiments shown in Figure 6 with statistical significance.

claim: AKAP79/150 is critical for anchoring PKA in dendritic spines through association with RII subunits.
source: AKAP79/150 is critical for anchoring PKA in dendritic spines (Tunquist et al., 2008; Weisenhaus et al., 2010) through association with RII subunits, which are the predominant neuronal PKA subunit in ~11 fold molar excess of C subunits in the CA1 neuropil (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by citations and quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RIIα is the major RII isoform in the CA1 neuropil.
source: Imaging studies (Ilouz et al., 2017; Weisenhaus et al., 2010) are consistent with our quantitative immunoblotting data, which show that RIIα is the major RII isoform in the CA1 neuropil.
evidence: Supported by citations to imaging studies and quantitative immunoblotting data from Figure 2.

claim: pRII dephosphorylation is limited prior to Ca2+ stimulation, enabling a tonic level of dissociated C subunits.
source: pRII dephosphorylation is limited prior to Ca2+ stimulation (Figure 7A), enabling a tonic level of dissociated C subunits sufficient to basally phosphorylate postsynaptic substrates in dendritic spines such as GluA1 subunits of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (Bear, 2003).
evidence: Inference illustrated in Figure 7A and supported by citation to literature on AMPA receptor regulation.

claim: LTD is brought about by CN, which is activated by Ca2+ entering spines through NMDA-type glutamate receptors.
source: LTD is brought about by CN (Mulkey et al., 1994), which is activated by Ca2+ entering spines through NMDA-type glutamate receptors (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study and illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: The PIAIIIT anchoring motif in AKAP79/150 is necessary for LTD.
source: AKAP79/150 contains a 'PIAIIIT' CN anchoring motif that is necessary for LTD (Jurado et al., 2010; Sanderson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on AKAP79/150 function in LTD.

claim: The PIAIIIT anchoring motif positions CN adjacent to pRII subunits where it can efficiently dephosphorylate them.
source: In addition to potentially targeting CN to postsynaptic substrates including GluA1 subunits, the PIAIIIT anchoring motif positions CN adjacent to pRII subunits where it can efficiently dephosphorylate them (Figure 7B).
evidence: Inference from the study's findings illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: CN dephosphorylation of pRII enables CN to increase the concentration of dephosphorylated RII species thereby directly suppressing PKA activity.
source: This enables CN to increase the concentration of dephosphorylated RII species (blue spheres in the kinetic scheme shown in Figure 7B) thereby directly suppressing PKA activity by increasing the rate of PKA C subunit capture.
evidence: Inference from the study's findings illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: Blocking regulation of RII phosphorylation state by introducing mutations reduces LTD in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Consistent with this mechanism, blocking regulation of RII phosphorylation state by introducing mutations that mimic either the phosphorylated or dephosphorylated forms of the IS reduces LTD in cultured hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by neuronal LTD experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: AKAP79 acts as a weak inhibitor of CN towards peptide substrates but enhances CN activity toward full-length pRII subunits.
source: First, previous studies showed that AKAP79 acts as a weak inhibitor of CN towards peptide substrates including a 20-mer peptide encompassing the phosphorylated RII IS (Coghlan et al., 1995; Kashishian et al., 1998), apparently at odds with the functional requirement for the anchoring protein in targeting CN to bring about LTD. We show that the key substrate for CN is likely to be full-length pRII subunits, and that in fact AKAP79 enhances the activity toward pRII at physiological concentrations by more than 10-fold.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figure 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: The PIAIIIT motif in AKAP79 includes an additional central residue compared to the typical PxIxIT motif.
source: A second enigmatic feature of AKAP79 is its CN anchoring motif, PIAIIIT, which includes an additional central residue compared to the typical PxIxIT motif (Roy and Cyert, 2009).
evidence: Structural information supported by citation to published review.

claim: In a crystal structure, the additional leucine in the PIAIIIT motif supports simultaneous binding of two copies of CN on either side of the motif.
source: In a crystal structure of CN in complex with a peptide corresponding to AKAP79 positions 336–346, the additional leucine supports simultaneous binding of two copies of CN on either side of the motif (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published structural study.

claim: Native mass spectrometry measurements support a stoichiometry of 2 CN to 1 AKAP79 in the AKAP79-CN-CaM-RIIα D/D complex.
source: Native mass spectrometry measurements of a purified AKAP79-CN-CaM-RIIα D/D complex also support a stoichiometry of 2 CN to 1 AKAP79 (Gold et al., 2011), although solution measurements indicate that when full-length RII subunits are bound to AKAP79, only one copy of CN can bind at a time (Li et al., 2012; Nygren et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published mass spectrometry and solution studies.

claim: CN may bind transiently to either side of the AKAP79 PIAIIIT motif enabling it to access both protomers of RII for efficient pRII dephosphorylation.
source: One possible explanation for this behavior is that CN binds transiently to either side of the AKAP79 PIAIIIT motif enabling it to access both protomers of RII anchored to AKAP79 for efficient pRII dephosphorylation (cartoon representations in Figure 7).
evidence: Speculative mechanism illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Mutating the PIAIIIT motif to a high-affinity canonical PxIxIT motif impairs the function of the phosphatase.
source: This idea is consistent with data showing that mutating the PIAIIIT motif to a high-affinity canonical PxIxIT motif impairs the function of the phosphatase (Li et al., 2012), although it should be noted that it is not possible to determine whether two-sided CN binding to AKAP79 is necessary using the data presented here.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study with acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: Existing models of AKAP79 function assume that CN overcomes PKA phosphorylation at substrates with no reduction in PKA phosphorylation rate.
source: Third, existing models of AKAP79 function assume that CN anchored to AKAP79 overcomes PKA phosphorylation at substrates with no reduction in PKA phosphorylation rate.
evidence: Statement about current models in the field.

claim: In the revised mechanism, CN directly suppresses PKA activity when removing phosphate from substrates primed by PKA thereby avoiding energetically costly futile cycling.
source: In our revised mechanism, CN directly suppresses PKA activity when removing phosphate from substrates primed by PKA thereby avoiding energetically costly ongoing futile cycling of phosphorylation and dephosphorylation by PKA and CN at these sites.
evidence: Inference from the study's findings proposing a revised model.

claim: AKAP79 is directly regulated by Ca2+/CaM, which binds to a 1-4-7-8 hydrophobic motif starting at position W79.
source: AKAP79 is directly regulated by Ca2+/CaM, which binds to a 1-4-7-8 hydrophobic motif (Patel et al., 2017) starting at position W79.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on AKAP79 regulation.

claim: Binding of Ca2+/CaM releases AKAP79 from the postsynaptic membrane.
source: Binding of Ca2+/CaM releases AKAP79 from the postsynaptic membrane (Dell'Acqua et al., 1998) and alters the conformation of the signaling complex by triggering formation of a second interface between CN and AKAP79 that involves an LxVP-type motif in AKAP79 (Gold et al., 2011; Nygren et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on AKAP79 regulation.

claim: Metal ions including Ca2+ alter rates of substrate binding and product release from PKA C subunits.
source: Furthermore, metal ions including Ca2+ alter rates of substrate binding and product release from PKA C subunits (Knape et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on PKA regulation by metal ions.

claim: Myristylation of C subunits is important for limiting their diffusion rate in dendritic spines and concentrating PKA activity at the cell membrane.
source: Myristylation of C subunits is important for limiting their diffusion rate in dendritic spines and concentrating PKA activity at the cell membrane (Tillo et al., 2017; Xiong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on C subunit localization.

claim: Localization of AKAP79 is regulated by palmitoylation at C36 and C139.
source: Localization of AKAP79 is also regulated by palmitoylation at C36 and C139 (Delint-Ramirez et al., 2011; Keith et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on AKAP79 palmitoylation.

claim: Palmitoylation is required for endosomal localization of AKAP79.
source: Palmitoylation is required for endosomal localization of AKAP79, and AKAP79 depalmitoylation and synaptic removal is additionally regulated by CaMKII (Woolfrey et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on AKAP79 localization.

claim: Removal of AKAP79 from synapses might be synchronized with accumulation of inhibited C subunits in the AKAP79 complex.
source: Our work suggests that removal of AKAP79 from synapses might be synchronized with accumulation of inhibited C subunits in the AKAP79 complex.
evidence: Speculative inference from the study's findings.

claim: C subunits do dissociate in neurons upon elevation of cAMP.
source: Current evidence indicates that C subunits do dissociate in neurons upon elevation of cAMP (Gold, 2019; Mo et al., 2017; Tillo et al., 2017), but it is important to note that suppression of PKA by pRII dephosphorylation is compatible with non-dissociative models of PKA activation and this might occur in certain physiological settings.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on PKA activation in neurons.

claim: AKAP79 is necessary for both induction of LTD of CA3-CA1 hippocampal synapses and for CN-mediated dephosphorylation of NFAT.
source: The anchoring protein is necessary for both induction of long-term depression (LTD) of CA3-CA1 hippocampal synapses (Lu et al., 2008; Tunquist et al., 2008; Weisenhaus et al., 2010), and for CN-mediated dephosphorylation of NFAT (Kar et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2014) – both processes that are driven by CN dephosphorylation of sites primed by PKA.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on AKAP79 function.

claim: Knockout of AKAP150 leads to the loss of cAMP oscillations in β-cells upon stimulation with insulin.
source: Oscillations of Ca2+, cAMP, and PKA activity have been observed in pancreatic β-cells (Hinke et al., 2012; Ni et al., 2011), and knockout of AKAP150 leads to the loss of cAMP oscillations in β-cells upon stimulation with insulin (Hinke et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on AKAP150 function in β-cells.

claim: CN dephosphorylation of pRII subunits bound to AKAP79 is likely to play a role in oscillatory patterns of PKA activity.
source: CN dephosphorylation of pRII subunits bound to AKAP79 is likely to play a role in oscillatory patterns of PKA activity, and it will be important to understand how this mechanism underlies responses to short-lived and oscillatory changes in Ca2+ and cAMP concentration.
evidence: Speculative inference about the role of the discovered mechanism in oscillatory signaling.

claim: AKAP79 underlies GABAA receptor regulation during LTD of GABAergic synapses.
source: For example, AKAP79 underlies GABAA receptor regulation during LTD of GABAergic synapses (Dacher et al., 2013), and it positions PKA and CN for regulation of TRPV channels (Zhang et al., 2008), Kv7 channels (Zhang and Shapiro, 2012), and β-adrenergic receptors (Houslay and Baillie, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on AKAP79 function in various contexts.

claim: AKAP79 is necessary for NFAT dephosphorylation following Ca2+ entry through both L-type calcium channels and the store-operated Ca2+ channel ORAI1.
source: AKAP79 is also necessary for NFAT dephosphorylation following Ca2+ entry through both L-type calcium channels (Wild et al., 2019) and the store-operated Ca2+ channel ORAI1 (Kar et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on AKAP79 function in NFAT regulation.

claim: The RII IS phosphorylation site is conserved throughout the animal kingdom.
source: The RII IS phosphorylation site is conserved throughout the animal kingdom, and co-anchoring of phosphatases alongside PKA is a feature of several AKAP complexes (Redden and Dodge-Kafka, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published review on AKAP complexes and established knowledge of sequence conservation.

claim: Additional anchoring proteins may be able to direct CN or other cellular phosphatases for direct suppression of PKA activity.
source: Future investigations may therefore explore whether additional anchoring proteins are able to direct CN – or other cellular phosphatases – for direct suppression of PKA activity.
evidence: Speculative statement about future research directions.
